what.text: Creatine is a compound the body makes and also gets from meat and fish. It is stored mainly in skeletal muscle, and also in heart muscle, brain and testes. The body breaks it down to creatinine, which leaves in the urine. Creatine monohydrate is the common supplement form, made by chemical synthesis.

src.label: FDA response letter to GRAS Notice 931 (creatine monohydrate)

what.text: Taking creatine raises the amount stored in muscle. In a 1999 trial, muscle creatine rose 22% after one week of supplements and stayed higher than with placebo for 12 weeks.

src.label: Volek JS, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc 1999

research.text: Creatine has been tested in many small randomized trials, mostly in men doing resistance training. Most found larger gains in strength and lean mass than training alone; some, including a trial in men with prostate cancer, found no added effect.
Each study is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Resistance-trained young men, 12 weeks

facts.v: 25 g a day for 1 week, then 5 g a day, with heavy resistance training
bench press and squat strength, fat-free mass, muscle fiber size, muscle creatine

research.found: Bench press rose 24% and squat 32% with creatine, compared with 16% and 24% with placebo. Body mass and fat-free mass rose more with creatine (6.3% vs about 3%). No side effects were reported.

src.label: Volek JS, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc 1999

research.title: Older men, resistance training, 12 weeks

facts.v: 30 men with a mean age of about 70 (16 creatine, 14 placebo)
a weight-based loading dose for 5 days, then a lower dose, with training three times a week
leg press, knee extension and bench press strength; lean tissue by DXA scan

research.found: Leg strength, endurance, power and lean tissue rose more with creatine (lean tissue +3.3 kg vs +1.3 kg). Bench press strength and fat mass changed similarly in both groups.

src.label: Chrusch MJ, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2001

research.meta: Men with prostate cancer · 2025 · Randomized, double-blind
research.title: Men with prostate cancer on hormone therapy, 12 weeks

facts.v: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; both groups did supervised resistance exercise 3 days a week
30 men aged 59 to 84 with prostate cancer on androgen deprivation therapy
lean mass, fat mass, strength and physical function

research.found: Both groups gained lean mass and strength, with no difference between creatine and placebo. No adverse events were reported from creatine or exercise.

src.label: Fairman CM, et al. J Sci Med Sport 2025

research.title: Hormones in college rugby players, 3 weeks

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with a 6-week washout
20 male college rugby players in season
25 g a day for 7 days, then 5 g a day for 14 days (with glucose), or glucose placebo

research.found: Testosterone did not change. DHT rose 56% after the first week and stayed 40% above baseline at 3 weeks. The authors said the long-term meaning is unknown. The study did not measure hair.

src.label: van der Merwe J, et al. Clin J Sport Med 2009

research.text: A 2024 meta-analysis of 23 trials in adults under 50 (most of them in men) found that creatine plus resistance training increased upper-body strength by about 4.4 kg and lower-body strength by about 11.4 kg more than placebo. Gains were seen in men but not significantly in women. One author has advised creatine makers.

src.label: Wang Z, et al. Nutrients 2024 (meta-analysis)

us.text: Creatine is sold in the US as a dietary supplement. FDA does not approve supplements before they are sold. FDA has also raised no questions about one maker’s conclusion that creatine monohydrate is safe (GRAS) for use in some foods. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: under US law, a dietary supplement can contain “a dietary substance for use by man to supplement the diet by increasing the total dietary intake.” FDA says it “does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed.”

src.label: 21 U.S.C. 321(ff), definition of dietary supplement, govinfo
Questions and answers on dietary supplements, FDA

items.text: in 2020 FDA replied “no questions” to a German ingredient maker’s notice that creatine monohydrate is generally recognized as safe (GRAS) in energy drinks, protein bars and powders, shakes, meal replacements, meat analogs and drink mixes, at about 1 g of creatine per serving. FDA stressed that its letter is not an affirmation of GRAS status.

world.lead: Creatine is sold without a prescription in the US (as a dietary supplement) and in Canada (as a licensed natural health product). It is not on the WADA Prohibited List.

side.text: In trials, creatine has caused few reported side effects. The most consistent change is weight gain. Health Canada requires a kidney warning on licensed products. FDA does not review supplements before sale.

items.text: body mass rose more with creatine than placebo in the 1999 trial; Health Canada requires products to warn that users may gain weight.

items.text: the GRAS notice cited human studies with no sign of liver or kidney harm at intakes up to 7 g a day for over a year and up to 25 g a day for 4 years, and an animal study with no kidney harm. These are the notifier’s summaries; FDA did not reach its own conclusion on them.
